new_statements.quote: 18. Each word in Luvale has one main stress, which is an important factor in correct word division. The stress of words in Bantu is typically on the penultimate syllable. Luvale modifies this rule as follows: A. Verbs 19. Verbs, being characteristically of two-syllable simple stems, are stressed on the first syllables of their roots, and in Luvale they retain that stress through all their forms and compounds, with the exceptions noted below. [...] B. Nouns 23. Nouns show the characteristic penultimate stress in the majority of cases. [...] 25. Polysyllabic nouns are usually stressed on the penult.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog's only record (StressTyp2, fixed-strict penult stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 (1 = a stressed syllable), quoting Horton 1949:18) rests on this very passage, and Horton's own words confirm penultimate stress as the general rule (para 18, nouns 23-25, other words 29). What the fragments add, and what the strict coding leaves out: main stress in verbs is bound to the root-initial syllable and stays there in derived/extended verbs (main stress then pre-penultimate, with only a secondary stress on the penult, paras 19, 22), deverbative nouns often keep that root stress (25), and monosyllabic roots stress the prefix (24). new_statements.rule_in_words: One main stress per word. Baseline is the Bantu penultimate stress, which Luvale 'modifies': (a) verbs carry main stress on the first syllable of the root (= the penult in a simple two-syllable stem such as ku-linga) and keep it there through derived and compound forms, so longer derived verbs have main stress before the penult; departures back to the penult occur in the subjunctive of derived forms, before the enclitic -nga, when a vowel-demonstrative coalesces with the verb, in vowel-verbs of more than two syllables and in some remote-past forms; monosyllabic verb stems keep penultimate stress by throwing it onto the prefix or by suffixation; (b) nouns are penultimate in the majority of cases: monosyllabic roots throw the stress onto the prefix (para 24, mutwe 'head'), polysyllabic nouns are usually penult, with exceptions (deverbatives usually, but not invariably, keep the root-syllable stress of the parent verb); (c) other words likewise penultimate, ideophones 'somewhat of a law to themselves'. A separate section (IV, paras 30-34) treats tone; para 25 mentions deverbatives 'with short vowels and high tone on the stressed syllable'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Para 22: 'Secondary stress occurs: a. Verb forms of more than [.] syllables after the main stress show a secondary stress on the penult: vahindukilile b. When the main stress of such a verb is drawn forward as in 21. a., b [..] normally stressed syllable retai[n]s a secondary stress' (p. 13); nouns: derived nouns of more than three syllables whose stress is drawn forward 'have a secondary stress', and 'Compound nouns have a secondary stress on [..]' (paras 26-28 fragments).
new_statements.exceptions: Verbs: root-initial main stress retained through all derived forms (para 19) except subjunctive of derived forms, enclitic -nga, coalesced vowel-demonstrative, vowel-verbs of 3+ syllables, some remote pasts (para 21 a-f); verbs in -ula/-una/-ola mentioned (para 21 d). Nouns: 'Monosyllabic roots throw the stress onto their prefixes, thus retaining the principle of penultimate stress' (24); 'some exceptions' to penult in polysyllabic nouns, chiefly deverbatives keeping root stress, e.g. kapopolweji (25); ideophones irregular (29).
new_statements.identity_note: Horton 1949 describes Luvale (Lwena, Lovale; Bantu K14) as spoken in the then Balovale district of Northern Rhodesia (Zambia) and adjacent Angola; no copy opened to confirm the dialect basis.
